'''Iphigenia Photaki''' ({{langx|el|Ιφιγένεια Φωτάκη}}, {{IPA|el|ifiˈʝeni.a foˈtaki|pron}}; also known after marriage as '''Iphigenia Vourvidou-Photaki''', {{langx|el|Ιφιγένεια Βουρβίδου-Φωτάκη}}; 1921–1983) was a [[Greeks|Greek]] [[Organic chemistry|organic chemist]] remembered for her contributions in [[Peptide synthesis|peptide chemical synthesis]], especially in the synthesis of biologically/[[Enzyme|enzymatically]] active peptides.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Iphigenia Vourvidou-Photaki|url=http://jupiter.chem.uoa.gr/thanost/fotaki/|access-date=12 Apr 2021|website=Laboratory of Physical Chemistry|publisher=University of Athens, Department of Chemistry|language=el|archive-date=12 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210412220114/http://jupiter.chem.uoa.gr/thanost/fotaki/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite book|url=http://jupiter.chem.uoa.gr/thanost/teax1957-2009.html|title=University Chemistry Professors (deceased after 1957)|publisher=Greek Association of Retired Chemists|year=2009|location=Athens|pages=21–22|language=el|script-title=el:Χημικοί Καθηγητές Α.Ε.Ι. (Αποβιώσαντες μετά το 1957)}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Kimourtzis|first1=P.|last2=Sigountou|first2=V.|date=2016|title=The era protons were gendered. Women in the Faculty of Sciences of the University of Athens (1922–1967)|url=https://pasithee.library.upatras.gr/academia/article/view/2307/2570|journal=Academia|location=Patras|publisher=Greek Higher Education Policy Network|volume=6|pages=79–132|eissn=2241-1402}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite book|url=http://jupiter.chem.uoa.gr/thanost/fotaki/Fotaki_cv_1968.pdf|title=Iphigenia Vourvidou-Photaki: Biographical Statement and Scientific Work|publisher=F. Konstantinidis & K. Mihalas|year=1968|location=Athens|pages=5–42|language=el|access-date=2021-04-13|archive-date=2021-04-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210412220140/http://jupiter.chem.uoa.gr/thanost/fotaki/Fotaki_cv_1968.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite book|url=http://jupiter.chem.uoa.gr/thanost/fotaki/Fotaki_cv_1976.pdf|title=Iphigenia Vourvidou-Photaki: Addendum to Biographical Statement and Scientific Work|publisher=K. Mihalas|year=1976|location=Athens|pages=3–23|language=el|access-date=2021-04-13|archive-date=2021-04-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210412220201/http://jupiter.chem.uoa.gr/thanost/fotaki/Fotaki_cv_1976.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Photaki was in 1965 the fourth woman overall to be [[Habilitation|habilitated]] in a scientific discipline in Greece, and the second to do so in the field of [[Chemistry]].<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> She specialised in peptide synthesis, influenced by her mentor and doctoral advisor [[Leonidas Zervas]], a global authority on the subject.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" /> After distinguished research in Basel, Athens, and later Cornell, Photaki eventually rose to Professor of Organic Chemistry and Head of the Laboratory of Organic Chemistry of the [[National and Kapodistrian University of Athens|University of Athens]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":4" />

== Biography ==

=== Early life, start of career and Basel ===
Photaki was born in [[Corinth (modern city)|Corinth]] in 1921 and finished her secondary education at the 2nd Girls' Gymnasium of [[Athens]] in 1938.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" /> In the same year she enrolled at the Department of Chemistry in the University of Athens, where she specialised in [[Organic chemistry]] under the mentorship of [[Leonidas Zervas]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> Her studies were interrupted during the [[Axis occupation of Greece]] when the Laboratory of Organic Chemistry was destroyed and Zervas was imprisoned as a member of the [[Greek Resistance]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /> Photaki was finally awarded her degree ''summa cum laude'' in 1946 and subsequently continued her postgraduate studies under Zervas, earning her [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in 1950 with a dissertation regarding [[glucosamine]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> Concurrently, she held a paid laboratory assistant position at the university already from 1943, carrying on as a research assistant until 1953.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

In 1953, Photaki was awarded a scholarship to conduct research in Basel after examinations by the Greek State Scholarships Foundation.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> At the [[University of Basel]] she worked in the Laboratory of Organic Chemistry, at the time headed by Nobel laureate [[Tadeusz Reichstein]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" /> For the first two years of her stay (1953–1955) she was part of the [[Max Brenner (chemist)|Max Brenner]] research group, later moving as an independent scientific associate of [[:de:Hans Erlenmeyer|Hans Erlenmeyer]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":2" /> Upon returning to Greece, she initially worked at the biochemical lab of the [[Evangelismos Hospital]] before being invited by Zervas to the nascent [[National Hellenic Research Foundation]] (NHRF) which he had helped found.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

=== Cornell and later career in Athens ===
Photaki was selected in 1962 by the US [[United States Department of Health and Human Services#Department of Health, Education, and Welfare|Department of Health, Education and Welfare]] among an international pool of candidates to conduct research by the side of Nobel laureate [[Vincent du Vigneaud]] at [[Cornell University]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> While in [[New York (state)|New York]], she also delivered a short series of lectures both in Cornell and at the [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH).<ref name=":2" />

Back in the University of Athens after Cornell, Photaki continued her research and was soon habilitated in 1965 following a thesis on [[oxytocin]], building on the work she started under du Vigneaud.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite thesis|last=Vourvidou-Photaki|first=Iphigenia|url=https://phdtheses.ekt.gr/eadd/handle/10442/14282|title=On Oxytocin|publisher=University of Athens, Department of Chemistry|year=1965|location=Athens|language=el|script-title=el:Περὶ Ὀξυτοκίνης|doi=10.12681/eadd/14282|type=Doctoral Dissertation |url-access=subscription|hdl=10442/hedi/14282|hdl-access=free}}</ref> Despite her internationally distinguished research and sizeable recent grants from the NHRF and the United States NIH, she was not allowed to teach by the [[Greek junta|Greek military junta]] until 1969 and was intensively interrogated by the [[Cities Police]] Security Directorate on account of her anti-dictatorial political beliefs.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

Photaki's teaching career was purposefully hindered by the [[Ministry of Education and Religious Affairs (Greece)|Ministry of Education]] until the [[Metapolitefsi|restoration of democracy]] in 1974; indeed, in 1975 she was promoted to extraordinary professor, a decade after receiving her habilitation.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":4" /> Shortly afterwards, in 1977, she was promoted to full professor (as Professor of Organic Chemistry) and Head of the Organic Chemistry Laboratory, both positions once held by her mentor Zervas.<ref name=":3" /> Photaki died in 1983 at the age of 62.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3" />

She was reported to spend very long hours at the laboratory, occasionally from "8 in the morning till 10 in the evening".<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":1" /> In her 20-year career as a member of the University of Athens faculty, she supervised (alone or jointly with other colleagues) more than 15 doctoral dissertations.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" />

== Scientific work ==
Although many of Photaki's important contributions were related to [[peptide synthesis]], her scientific work touched on a large number of topics within [[organic synthesis]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" /> In total she published around 50 papers in international English- or German-language chemical journals.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" />

=== Peptide synthesis ===
Continuing and expanding the tradition of the University of Athens within the subject, starting from Zervas of [[Bergmann-Zervas carbobenzoxy method]] fame, Photaki initially worked on further refinement of suitable [[protecting group]]s for [[oligopeptide]] synthesis.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" /> She investigated with Zervas new types of protection such as ''N''-protection with benzyl [[Organophosphate|phosphate esters]] (''N''-phosphamide derivatives), ''S''-protection using [[Triphenylmethane|trityl]], [[Benzhydryl compounds|benzhydryl]] or [[Benzoyl group|benzoyl]] groups (as part of the greater effort for the synthesis of asymmetric [[cysteine]]-containing peptides), ''N''-protection using the [[O-nitrophenylsulfenyl group|''o''-nitrophenylsulfenyl]] (NPS) group discovered in their Athens laboratory, or ''S''-protection using the ''p''-methoxycarbobenzoxy group (a modification of the [[Benzyl chloroformate|Z group]]).<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" />

With the above methodologies she embarked on the synthesis of complex polypeptides, especially fragments of enzyme active sites and peptide hormones.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" /> Some notable achievements in papers Photaki co-authored include the first synthesis of the 20-membered [[insulin]] intra-chain ring or –following her research under du Vigneaud– several previously inaccessible [[oxytocin]] analogues (''e.g.'' 4-deamido-oxytocin) and a novel oxytocin synthesis ''via'' a different route than the du Vigneaud synthesis.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" />

In later years she also examined the preparation of biologically active [[Isopeptide bond|atypical peptides]] such as ''N''<sup>ω</sup>-arginine or [[lanthionine]]-containing peptides.<ref name=":4" />

=== Other research ===
With her expertise on peptide synthesis, Photaki examined the [[Biocatalysis|biocatalytic]] properties and [[Chemical kinetics|kinetics]] of enzyme [[active site]] analogues she prepared.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" />

Another research topic she developed in the early part of her career was the chemical transformation of [[carbohydrate]]s and [[Glycosylation|glycosylated]] species, such as the [[Stereoselectivity|stereoselective]] conversion of <small>D</small>-[[glucosamine]] to <small>L</small>-[[Serine|serinaldehyde]] which formed the basis of her doctoral thesis.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

Finally, she examined some of the [[coordination complex]]es formed by [[histidine]]-containing peptides with {{Chem|Cu|2+}}, {{Chem|Co|2+}}, {{Chem|Zn|2+}} and {{Chem|Ce|4+}}, and after the [[Chemotherapy|antitumour]] properties of platinum complexes were realised, she also worked on the peptide enzymatic reactions in the presence of {{Chem|Pt|2+}} amine complexes.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" />

== Honours and awards ==
In 1970 Iphigenia Vourvidou-Photaki was awarded the one-off Georgios Panopoulos Prize of the [[Academy of Athens (modern)|Academy of Athens]], presented to her for "...her research on the chemical synthesis of polypeptide hormones and investigation of enzyme active sites, which constitute an internationally notable contribution of Greek science to the modern discipline of Chemistry".<ref name=":4" />

During her lifetime, she was invited many times as a distinguished researcher in academic conferences related to her subject; some examples were the personal invitations she received to the 3rd European Peptide Symposium (EPS) (Basel, 1960), the 5th EPS (Oxford, 1962), 6th EPS (Athens, 1963 as organiser), 6th International Biochemistry Conference (New York, 1964), 7th EPS (Budapest, 1964), Symposium on Natural Sulfur Compounds (Copenhagen, 1966), NATO Seminar of Molecular Biology (Spetses, 1966), 8th EPS (Noordwijk, 1966), 9th EPS (Paris, 1968), 10th EPS (Abano, 1970), 11th EPS (Vienna, 1971), 3rd American Peptide Symposium (APS) (Boston, 1972), 13th EPS (Kiryat, 1974), 4th APS (New York, 1975), and the 14th EPS (Wépion, 1976) over which she presided.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" />
